title: NEC Past Paper - Set 16 (2083 Asoj 18, 3rd shift)

questions.q: Kulekhani is which type of dam?
questions.s: Kulekhani I is a rock-fill dam with a sloping clay core — Nepal's only storage (reservoir) hydropower scheme.
questions.trap: "Concrete-faced rock-fill" (CFRD) is also a rock-fill dam, so both look right; Kulekhani uses an internal clay core, not a concrete facing.
questions.trick: Nepal has one storage project and one rock-fill dam, and they are the same thing.

questions.q: Which type of toilet is suitable where water is scarce?
questions.s: A composting latrine needs no water at all — excreta decompose aerobically with ash or sawdust. Every flush-based system needs a reliable water supply.
questions.trap: Pour-flush uses only 1-2 litres, so it reads as the water-saving option; "scarce" means none available, which only composting satisfies.
questions.trick: Read "water scarce" as "zero water", then only one option survives.

questions.q: Which risk can be controlled by neither the owner nor the contractor?
questions.s: Force majeure covers earthquake, flood and war — outside the control of both parties, which is why contracts relieve both rather than allocate it.
questions.trap: Market risk also feels uncontrollable, but it is allocated to one party by the contract; force majeure is excused for both.
questions.trick: Ask which risk the contract *excuses* rather than *assigns*.
questions.mn: Force majeure = nobody's fault, nobody's risk.

questions.q: In RCC, the stiffness of the concrete material is expressed in terms of:
questions.s: Modulus of elasticity Ec = 5000√fck (IS 456) relates direct stress to strain and is the stiffness used in RCC design.
questions.trap: Modulus of rupture is also a concrete property (flexural tensile strength, 0.7√fck) — it is a strength, not a stiffness.
questions.trick: Rupture and resilient are strengths; elasticity and rigidity are stiffnesses, and rigidity is for shear.
questions.mn: E for extension, G for shear, rupture for cracking.

questions.q: In a cantilever beam carrying any load, both the shear force and the bending moment are zero at the:
questions.s: Nothing lies beyond the free end, so there is no force or moment to carry there. Both maxima occur at the fixed support instead.
questions.trap: At a point of contraflexure the *moment* is zero but the shear is not; the question demands both.
questions.trick: Cut just inside the free end — there is nothing outboard to equilibrate.

questions.q: An outlet whose discharge depends only on the water level in the distributary channel is a:
questions.s: A semi-module (flexible outlet) discharges according to the distributary (upstream) level only, and is independent of the watercourse level downstream.
questions.trap: A modular outlet is independent of *both* levels; a non-modular one depends on both. Only the semi-module depends on exactly one.
questions.trick: Count the levels it depends on: 2 = non-modular, 1 = semi-modular, 0 = modular.

questions.q: The tenure of the Nepal Engineering Council is:
questions.s: The NEC Act 2055 fixes the tenure of the Council at four years.
questions.trap: Five years is the tenure of several other Nepali statutory bodies, which makes it the natural wrong guess.
questions.trick: NEC and its chairman both run on a four-year term.
questions.mn: NEC: Four letters after N-E-C... four years.

questions.q: Permissible stress is the basis of design in the:
questions.s: The working stress method keeps the actual stress below a permissible stress obtained by dividing the yield (or crushing) stress by a factor of safety.
questions.trap: Limit state design also uses a material factor, but it reduces the *characteristic strength*; only WSM speaks of permissible stress.
questions.trick: Permissible stress ⇒ elastic ⇒ working stress method.

questions.q: The early strength of cement is due to the compound:
questions.s: C3S hydrates quickly and gives the strength gained up to about 28 days. C2S hydrates slowly and supplies the later, ultimate strength.
questions.trap: C3A sets fastest of all, but it contributes flash set and heat rather than strength — gypsum is added to retard it.
questions.trick: 3 before 2: C3S early, C2S late.
questions.mn: C3S = Starts strong; C2S = Slow and steady.

questions.q: The arrangement made to support an unsafe structure temporarily is known as:
questions.s: Shoring props a wall or structure that is in danger of collapse until permanent repair is carried out.
questions.trap: Underpinning also saves an unsafe structure — but it strengthens the *foundation* permanently rather than propping temporarily.
questions.trick: Shore = support sideways; underpin = support from below; scaffold = support the workmen.

questions.q: Before plastering, the surface should be:
questions.s: The surface is cleaned of dust and loose mortar and then wetted, so it does not draw mixing water out of the fresh plaster and cause it to crack.
questions.trap: "Rough" is half right — joints are raked to give a key — but the stated requirement before applying plaster is clean and wet.
questions.trick: A dry background steals the water the plaster needs to hydrate.
questions.mn: Clean it, wet it, plaster it.

questions.q: The drawback of electrical seasoning of timber is that it:
o: Is costly and may split the timber
questions.s: Electrical seasoning is rapid and uniform but expensive, and the rapid moisture loss can split or check the timber.
questions.trap: Rapid and uniform seasoning are the *advantages* of the method, offered here as if they were faults.
questions.trick: The fastest seasoning method is also the most expensive and the most violent.

questions.q: The initial setting time of ordinary Portland cement is:
questions.s: IS 269 requires an initial setting time of not less than 30 minutes, and a final setting time of not more than 600 minutes (10 hours).
questions.trap: 600 minutes is the *final* setting time; candidates who remember only one number often give it here.
questions.trick: Initial is a minimum (30 min), final is a maximum (600 min).

questions.q: The indentation or depression on the surface of a brick is called a:
questions.s: The frog is the depression in the larger face; it keys the mortar and carries the maker's mark. It is laid uppermost.
questions.trap: Header, stretcher and closer all describe how a brick is *laid*, not a feature on it.
questions.trick: Only one of the four names a shape cut into the brick itself.
questions.mn: The frog sits in a hollow.

questions.q: When water is added to cement, heat is:
questions.s: Hydration is exothermic — about 500 kJ/kg of cement. The heat is useful in cold weather and a problem in mass concrete.
questions.trap: Concrete feels cool and damp while curing, which makes "absorbed" sound plausible.
questions.trick: If hydration absorbed heat, mass concrete would not need cooling pipes.

questions.q: For a given water-cement ratio, the strength of concrete and the fineness modulus of the aggregate are:
questions.s: A higher fineness modulus means coarser aggregate, which needs less water and less paste for the same workability, so strength rises.
questions.trap: "Finer is better" is the instinct, but finer aggregate has more surface area and demands more water.
questions.trick: Higher FM → coarser → less water demand → stronger.

questions.q: An increase in the fineness modulus of an aggregate means the aggregate is:
questions.s: Fineness modulus is the sum of the cumulative percentages retained on the standard sieves divided by 100 — a bigger number means more material retained, hence coarser.
questions.trap: The name says "fineness", so a higher value reads as finer; it is the opposite.
questions.trick: It measures what is *retained*, not what passes.

questions.q: Beyond the minimum water-cement ratio needed for workability, further water makes the strength of concrete:
questions.s: Water beyond that needed for hydration and placing leaves capillary voids when it evaporates, and strength falls roughly with Abrams' law.
questions.trap: Below the minimum, more water does help — because the mix cannot be compacted at all. The question asks about beyond it.
questions.trick: Every litre of surplus water becomes a void.
questions.mn: More water, more voids, less strength.

questions.q: In a meandering channel, the intake length should be:
o: The length of one full loop
A straight reach of the channel
questions.s: An intake is sited on a straight reach, where the flow is symmetrical and the sediment distribution predictable; a bend throws sediment to the inside.
questions.trap: "Length of one loop" sounds technical but a loop is exactly the curved reach to be avoided.
questions.trick: Intakes dislike bends — the outer bank scours and the inner bank silts.

questions.q: Which structure prevents floating debris from damaging the gates and the weir?
questions.s: A trash rack is a steel grille across the intake that stops logs and floating rubbish from reaching the gates and turbines.
questions.trap: Energy dissipators also protect downstream works — against *water* energy, not debris.
questions.trick: Debris is a solid problem and needs a solid screen.

questions.q: Lacey's silt factor for a mean particle diameter of 0.7 mm is approximately:
questions.trap: 1.76 is the value for d = 1 mm, and it is also the constant in the formula — so it is the easiest wrong answer to pick.
questions.trick: d < 1 mm gives f < 1.76; d > 1 mm gives f > 1.76.
questions.mn: f = 1.76√d — root of d, not d itself.

questions.q: Lacey's silt factor for a mean particle diameter of 0.343 mm is approximately:
questions.trap: 0.586 is √0.343 — the intermediate step, left there as an option for anyone who forgets to multiply by 1.76.
questions.trick: Take the root first, then multiply; never the other way round.

questions.q: If a man weighs 120 N on the earth, his weight on the moon is about:
questions.s: Lunar gravity is about one-sixth of the earth's, so 120/6 = 20 N. The mass is unchanged.
questions.trap: 720 N is 120 × 6 — the right factor applied the wrong way.
questions.trick: The moon is smaller, so the weight must be smaller.

questions.q: Dissolved iron is removed from water by:
questions.s: Aeration oxidises soluble ferrous iron to insoluble ferric hydroxide, which is then settled and filtered out.
questions.trap: Alum is the standard coagulant, so it is the reflex answer — but it cannot remove iron that is still dissolved.
questions.trick: Dissolved iron must be made insoluble first, and oxygen is what does it.

questions.q: The best way to find the position of the water table at a site is:
questions.s: An observation (monitoring) well is left open in the ground and the water level read directly once it stabilises.
questions.trap: SPT boreholes do reveal water, but the reading is disturbed by drilling fluid and is taken only in passing.
questions.trick: To measure a water level, measure the water level.
questions.mn: Observe the water in an observation well.

questions.q: The immediate settlement of a cohesive soil is given by:
questions.s: Elastic settlement is proportional to the pressure q and width B, and inversely proportional to the modulus Es, with (1 − μ²) for lateral restraint.
questions.trap: The sign inside the bracket is the whole question: (1 + μ²) appears in no elastic settlement formula.
questions.trick: Settlement must grow with load and shrink with stiffness, which rules out the inverted option at once.
questions.mn: q B over E, times one minus mu squared.

questions.q: The crest of a siphon spillway is fixed at:
questions.s: The crest sits at full reservoir level so the siphon primes and begins to discharge the moment the reservoir rises above FRL.
questions.trap: "Maximum water level" is above FRL — setting the crest there would delay operation until the dam was already overtopping.
questions.trick: A spillway must start working exactly when storage is full.

questions.q: The output power of a turbine depends upon:
questions.s: P = ρgQHη — the discharge, the net head and the efficiency together. The type of turbine matters only through the efficiency it achieves.
questions.trap: "Head and type of turbine" omits discharge, without which there is no power at all.
questions.trick: Write the formula before reading the options.
questions.mn: Power = γQHη: discharge, head and efficiency, all three.

questions.q: The hire and tool charges are typically taken as what percentage of the unskilled labour cost?
questions.s: Standard Nepali rate analysis adds about 3% of the unskilled labour cost for tools and plant hire.
questions.trap: Contractor's profit (10-15%) and overheads are larger percentages and get confused with this small one.
questions.trick: Tools are a small addition — the smallest percentage offered is the right instinct here.
questions.mn: Tools 3%, profit 10-15% — the small one is the tools.

questions.q: The contour interval is:
questions.s: A large-scale map (small denominator, more detail) uses a small contour interval; a small-scale map uses a large one.
questions.trap: "Directly proportional" is chosen by anyone who confuses map scale with ground area covered.
questions.trick: More detail on the sheet means contours closer together in value.

questions.q: Which depth is used in the Froude number for an open channel?
questions.s: Fr = V/√(gD) where D is the hydraulic depth, A/T — the area divided by the top width.
questions.trap: For a wide rectangular channel the hydraulic depth equals the flow depth, which makes "flow depth" look right in general; it is not.
questions.trick: Hydraulic depth is area over top width, and that is what the celerity of a wave depends on.

questions.q: A subtense bar is typically used to determine:
o: Short distances up to about 200 m
Very short distances of a few centimetres
questions.s: A 2 m horizontal subtense bar is sighted with a theodolite and the distance computed from the subtended angle — accurate to about 200 m.
questions.trap: A kilometre sounds plausible for a tacheometric method, but the angle becomes too small to read accurately beyond about 200 m.
questions.trick: A 2 m bar at 200 m already subtends under 35 minutes.
questions.mn: Subtense bar: short bar, short range.

questions.q: The first watering given to a crop when it is a few centimetres high is called:
questions.s: Kor watering is the first watering after the plants have appeared; its depth is the kor depth and its duration the kor period.
questions.trap: Paleo is also a "first" watering — but it is given *before* sowing, not after the crop is up.
questions.trick: Paleo comes before the plant; kor comes after it shows.

questions.q: Which correction is NOT applied to the standard penetration test value?
questions.s: SPT N-values are corrected for overburden pressure, for dilatancy in fine saturated sands and for energy losses. The meniscus correction belongs to a capillary rise or hydrometer reading.
questions.trap: "Meniscus" is a genuine soils-laboratory correction, just from a different test — which is exactly why it is offered.
questions.trick: Ask which correction has nothing to do with driving a split spoon into the ground.
questions.mn: Meniscus is a glass tube, not a borehole.

questions.q: Cavitation bubbles collapse when they move into a region of:
questions.s: Bubbles form where the pressure falls to the vapour pressure and implode violently when carried into a higher-pressure zone — which is what pits the runner.
questions.trap: Low pressure is where cavitation *starts*; the question asks where the bubbles collapse.
questions.trick: Form low, collapse high.
questions.mn: Born in the low, die in the high.

questions.q: In the unconfined compression test, the corrected area of cross-section at any strain ε is:
questions.s: The sample shortens and bulges at constant volume, so the area must grow: dividing by (1 − ε) is what makes it grow.
questions.trap: Multiplying by (1 − ε) gives a shrinking area, which would mean the sample got thinner as it was squashed.
questions.trick: Compression fattens the specimen, so the corrected area is larger than the original.
questions.mn: Squash it, it spreads — divide, don't multiply.

questions.q: The presence of alumina in brick earth gives the brick:
questions.s: Alumina makes the clay plastic so it can be moulded. In excess it causes shrinkage and warping on drying.
questions.trap: Iron oxide gives the red colour and silica gives hardness and resistance to shrinkage — each option belongs to a different constituent.
questions.trick: Alumina is the clay mineral itself, and clay is what makes earth plastic.
questions.mn: Alumina = plasticity; silica = strength; iron = colour.

questions.q: In a high-strength friction-grip bolted connection, the load is transferred mainly by:
questions.s: The bolt is tightened to a high pre-tension, clamping the plates; the load passes through the friction at the interface, not through the bolt shank.
questions.trap: Ordinary black bolts do transfer load by shear and bearing, which makes shear the habitual answer.
questions.trick: The name says it: high-strength *friction grip*.
questions.mn: HSFG = Held by Surface Friction Grip.

questions.q: How is salinity removed from soil?
questions.s: Leaching washes the salts down through the profile, but only drainage carries the saline water away. Without it the salts simply return as the water evaporates.
questions.trap: Flooding alone is half the answer and is offered on its own; without drainage it eventually makes salinity worse.
questions.trick: Salt must leave the site, not just move down and come back.
questions.mn: Leach and drain — both or neither.

questions.q: In the repair of potholes, the surrounding portion of the pavement is cut out in what shape?
questions.s: The patch is cut to a rectangle with vertical faces and sides parallel and perpendicular to the centre line, so the new material can be compacted against a straight edge.
questions.trap: A pothole is irregular, so cutting it "as found" seems economical — but a feathered edge fails again at once.
questions.trick: Compaction needs a square shoulder to work against.

questions.q: To attain the required shape of a tunnel, the holes blasted last are the:
questions.s: Trimmers (perimeter holes) are fired last and define the finished profile. Cut holes open the free face first and easers enlarge it.
questions.trap: Cut holes are fired *first* and are the best known of the three, so they are the reflex answer.
questions.trick: The holes that shape the edge must be the ones nearest the edge.
questions.mn: Cut, ease, trim — trim shapes it.

questions.q: Which structure heads up water for an adequate supply into an off-taking channel?
questions.s: A cross regulator is built across the parent channel to raise its level so that the off-take draws its full share.
questions.trap: The head regulator controls the off-take itself — it admits water, but it cannot raise the level in the parent canal.
questions.trick: To raise a level you must obstruct the main flow, which only the cross regulator does.
questions.mn: Cross it to raise it; head it to take it.

questions.q: In a network diagram, a dummy activity is:
o: A logical connection consuming no time or resources
An activity of very short duration
An activity on the critical path
questions.s: A dummy shows a dependency, or keeps two activities from sharing the same start and end nodes. It consumes neither time nor resources.
questions.trap: It is drawn as a dashed arrow, which makes "geometrical" tempting — but its purpose is logic, not drafting.
questions.trick: A dummy has zero duration, so it can never add to a path length.

questions.q: The factor (1 + i)⁻ⁿ is called the:
questions.s: It converts a single future sum to its value today, so it is the single-payment present worth (discount) factor.
questions.trap: (1 + i)ⁿ — the same expression with a positive exponent — is the compound amount factor, offered right beside it.
questions.trick: A negative exponent always discounts backwards to the present.
questions.mn: Minus n = minus time = present worth.

questions.q: In a waterlogged area under irrigation, which type of drainage is used?
questions.s: Perforated tile or pipe drains laid below the root zone lower the water table — surface drains remove only ponded water, not a high water table.
questions.trap: Surface drainage is the obvious treatment for standing water, but waterlogging is a groundwater problem.
questions.trick: Waterlogging is measured by the depth of the water table, so the cure must be sub-surface.
questions.mn: Water table high → tile drain deep.

questions.q: A Bourdon gauge measures:
questions.s: The tube is open to the atmosphere on the outside, so it reads the difference from atmospheric — gauge pressure, zero when open to air.
questions.trap: A Bourdon gauge can indeed read a vacuum, but only as negative gauge pressure; "only" makes that option wrong.
questions.trick: If it reads zero in open air, it is a gauge instrument.
questions.mn: Bourdon reads gauge, add Patm for absolute.

questions.q: In a construction project, sponsors are those who:
questions.s: The sponsor finances the project and carries the commercial risk; the owner is whoever holds the asset afterwards, and the two need not be the same.
questions.trap: Sponsor and owner are the same party on many small projects, which makes "owner" look equally correct.
questions.trick: Sponsorship is about money, not about title.

questions.q: A project is acceptable on economic grounds when:
questions.s: Benefits must exceed costs for the project to be worth doing. B/C = 1 only breaks even and leaves nothing for risk.
questions.trap: B/C = 1 is the boundary and is often listed as "acceptable"; strictly it is the marginal case, not an acceptable one.
questions.trick: Would you build something that returns exactly what it costs?

questions.q: Rutting in a flexible pavement is caused by:
o: Deformation accumulating in the subgrade and the layers above it
Tension at the bottom of the bituminous layer
questions.s: Rutting is a permanent vertical deformation in the wheel path, produced by repeated loading compacting and shearing the subgrade and the unbound layers.
questions.trap: Tension at the bottom of the bituminous layer is the cause of *fatigue cracking*, the other classic flexible-pavement failure.
questions.trick: Rutting is a shape change (vertical strain); fatigue is a crack (tensile strain).

questions.q: The power required to drive a pump is given by:
questions.s: The water power is γQH; the shaft power is larger because of losses, so it is divided by the efficiency.
questions.trap: γQH alone is the *output* (water) power — correct for the water, wrong for the motor.
questions.trick: Input power is always greater than output, so efficiency goes underneath for a pump.
questions.mn: Pump: divide by η. Turbine: multiply by η.

questions.q: For maximum parking capacity along a given kerb length, parking should be at:
questions.s: Right-angle (perpendicular) parking fits the most vehicles into a given kerb length; parallel parking fits the fewest but needs the least depth.
questions.trap: 45° parking is easier to enter and is commonly used, so it is remembered as the "best" arrangement.
questions.trick: The steeper the angle, the more cars and the more depth required.

questions.q: When a jet of water strikes a stationary inclined plate, the water:
o: Comes to rest on the plate
questions.s: A smooth plate takes only the normal component of momentum; the tangential component is unchanged, so the water runs along the surface.
questions.trap: "Perpendicular to the plate" describes the *force* on the plate, not the motion of the water.
questions.trick: Separate the force (normal) from the flow (tangential).

questions.q: The daily average traffic obtained from a 30-day survey within a year is called:
questions.s: ADT is the average over any period shorter than a year. Only a full 365-day count gives AADT.
questions.trap: AADT is the better-known term and is the one most candidates reach for first.
questions.trick: The extra A in AADT stands for annual — and 30 days is not a year.
questions.mn: Less than a year = ADT only.

questions.q: The two parameters measured in the Marshall stability test are:
questions.s: The specimen is loaded diametrically at 50 mm/min at 60 °C; the peak load is the stability and the deformation at that load is the flow value.
questions.trap: Density and voids are computed from the same specimen, so they feel like the measured parameters — they are derived, not measured in the test itself.
questions.trick: The test is named after the stability; the flow is the other half of the same reading.

questions.q: As per NRS 2070, the maximum value of the coefficient of lateral friction is taken as:
questions.s: The design value of lateral (side) friction is 0.15, used with the superelevation in e + f = V²/127R.
questions.trap: 0.35-0.40 is the *longitudinal* friction coefficient used for braking distance — a different number for a different direction.
questions.trick: Sideways friction is small; braking friction is large.

questions.q: The length of road visible ahead to a driver at any instant is called:
questions.s: Sight distance is the general term for the visible length of road; stopping, overtaking and intermediate are particular sight distances defined for particular purposes.
questions.trap: Stopping sight distance is the one most used in design, so it is the first that comes to mind.
questions.trick: The question defines the family, not a member of it.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a stage of soil exploration?
questions.s: Exploration runs reconnaissance → preliminary → detailed, and is complete before construction begins.
questions.trap: Soil is certainly inspected as the excavation opens up, but that is construction supervision, not a stage of exploration.
questions.trick: Exploration informs the design; it cannot happen after the design is built.

questions.q: The process dealing with vertical curves and gradients is called:
questions.s: Vertical alignment is the longitudinal profile — gradients and the summit and valley curves joining them.
questions.trap: "Geometric design" covers both alignments and is a legitimate description, but it is not specific to the vertical one.
questions.trick: Gradients and vertical curves are seen in elevation, not in plan.

questions.q: Which structure prevents floating and submerged debris from entering the water conductor system?
questions.s: The trash rack screens the intake. A silt excluder deals with sediment, which is carried in suspension rather than floating.
questions.trap: A silt excluder also keeps unwanted material out, but silt is not debris and passes straight through a rack.
questions.trick: Rack for solids you can see, excluder for particles you cannot.
questions.mn: Rack catches rubbish, excluder catches silt.

questions.q: The axis of a dam is generally defined as the line along the:
o: Crown of the dam on the upstream side
questions.s: The axis is the line of the crest (crown) on the upstream edge; it is the reference from which the whole layout is set out.
questions.trap: The centre of the base is the natural geometric guess and is wrong — the axis is defined at the top, not the bottom.
questions.trick: The axis is what you would peg out first on site, and that is the crest line.
questions.mn: Axis = upstream edge of the crest.

questions.q: Which of the following is a high-head turbine?
questions.s: Pelton is an impulse turbine for heads above about 300 m. Francis suits medium heads and Kaplan low heads.
questions.trap: "Reaction turbine" is sometimes offered as an option; it is a class, not a turbine, and covers both Francis and Kaplan.
questions.trick: Head order: Pelton high, Francis medium, Kaplan low.

questions.q: For a given discharge, the efficiency of a sedimentation basin is increased by:
questions.s: Removal depends on the overflow rate Q/A, so a larger surface area gives a lower overflow rate and better settling. Depth does not enter it.
questions.trap: A deeper tank holds more water and gives a longer detention time, which sounds like better settling — but a particle must still fall faster than the overflow rate.
questions.trick: Settling is governed by area, not by volume.
questions.mn: Q over A, never Q over V.

questions.q: The function of a surge tank is to:
o: Relieve water hammer pressure in the penstock
Increase the pressure in the penstock
Increase the discharge to the turbine
questions.s: On sudden gate closure the surge tank gives the decelerating water somewhere to go, keeping the pressure rise out of the tunnel and penstock.
questions.trap: A forebay also sits on the conveyance line and stores water, but it regulates supply rather than absorbing a surge.
questions.trick: Surge tank = shock absorber on the waterway.

questions.q: Power available continuously throughout the year in a hydropower project is called:
questions.s: Firm (primary) power is what the scheme can guarantee even in the driest period. Anything above it is secondary and seasonal.
questions.trap: Installed capacity is the largest number on the project and is often mistaken for what the plant actually delivers.
questions.trick: Firm power is set by the worst month, not the best.

questions.q: A canal drop or fall is provided when:
o: The ground slope exceeds the designed bed slope
The ground slope is less than the designed bed slope
The ground slope equals the bed slope
questions.s: Where the ground falls faster than the canal needs to, the surplus level is taken out in a vertical drop so the canal keeps its design slope without excessive cutting.
questions.trap: The reverse case — ground flatter than the canal — calls for filling or a different alignment, not a fall.
questions.trick: Ground steeper than canal ⇒ shed the extra height in one step.

questions.q: An outlet is said to be proportional when its flexibility is:
questions.s: Flexibility is the ratio of the rate of change of outlet discharge to that of the distributary. At unity the outlet takes a constant share of whatever the parent canal carries.
questions.trap: Flexibility greater than unity (hyper-proportional) sounds like "more proportional"; it means the outlet over-responds.
questions.trick: Proportional means the share does not change, so the ratio must be exactly one.

questions.q: The structure provided upstream of the head regulator to keep silt out of the canal is a:
questions.s: A silt excluder works in the river upstream of the head regulator and prevents silt from entering. A silt ejector removes silt that has already entered the canal.
questions.trap: Excluder and ejector differ by one word and by where they sit — the commonest confusion in this chapter.
questions.trick: Exclude before entry, eject after entry.
questions.mn: Excluder keeps out, ejector throws out.

questions.q: A hydraulic structure that allows drainage water to join the canal is called a:
questions.s: An inlet admits the drainage of a small stream into the canal where carrying it separately would not be worth the structure.
questions.trap: A canal escape does the opposite — it lets surplus canal water out into a drain.
questions.trick: Inlet in, escape out.

questions.q: The maximum permissible (non-scouring) velocity in a sewer is generally:
questions.s: Above about 3 m/s the sewage scours the invert. The minimum self-cleansing velocity at the other end of the range is about 0.6 m/s.
questions.trap: 0.6 m/s is the *minimum* self-cleansing velocity and is the number most often memorised.
questions.trick: One number stops silting, the other stops scouring — 0.6 and 3.0.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of Manning's roughness coefficient n is:
questions.s: From V = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2), n must carry the dimensions L^(−1/3)T to make the equation homogeneous.
questions.trap: Manning's n is often called a "coefficient", which suggests it is dimensionless — it is not.
questions.trick: Chezy's C is L^(1/2)T⁻¹; Manning's n is its awkward cousin, L^(−1/3)T.
questions.mn: n has dimensions; only Fr and Re do not.

questions.q: The dimension of Chezy's coefficient C is:
questions.s: V = C√(RS) with S dimensionless, so C = V/√R has dimensions L^(1/2)T⁻¹.
questions.trap: L^(−1/3)T is Manning's n, sitting right beside it — the two are routinely swapped.
questions.trick: C multiplies a square root of length, so it must carry a half power.

questions.q: The angle between a principal plane and the plane of maximum shear is:
questions.s: On Mohr's circle the principal points and the maximum-shear points are 90° apart, which is 45° in the physical element.
questions.trap: 90° is the angle on the circle, and it is offered precisely to catch anyone who forgets to halve it.
questions.trick: Always halve a Mohr's circle angle to get the real one.
questions.mn: 90 on the circle, 45 on the steel.

questions.q: The cylinder strength of concrete is lower than the cube strength because of:
o: The aspect ratio of the specimen and the end restraint
questions.s: The cube is short and squat, so platen friction confines it and raises the apparent strength. The taller cylinder (h/d = 2) escapes that restraint and reads about 0.8 of the cube value.
questions.trap: All the other options change the concrete itself, when the specimens are cast from the same mix.
questions.trick: Same concrete, different shape — so the cause must be geometric.

questions.q: The binding wire required for 1 quintal (100 kg) of reinforcement is about:
questions.s: Standard rate analysis allows roughly 1 kg of binding wire per quintal of steel, i.e. about 1%.
questions.trap: The figures 0.5 and 1.5 bracket the right one and all look equally plausible without the rule of thumb.
questions.trick: One kilogram per quintal is one per cent — easy to carry into the hall.
questions.mn: One kilogram of wire per quintal of steel, so one per cent.

questions.q: In a cantilever beam carrying a downward load, which statement is correct?
o: The top is in tension and the bottom in compression
The top is in compression and the bottom in tension
questions.s: A cantilever hogs, so the beam is convex upwards at the support: the top fibres stretch and the steel goes at the top.
questions.trap: A simply supported beam does the opposite, and that is the picture most candidates carry.
questions.trick: Sketch the deflected shape — the stretched face is the tension face.

questions.q: The deflection at the centre of a fixed beam carrying a uniformly distributed total load W over span L is:
questions.s: Fixing both ends reduces the simply supported value 5WL³/384EI by a factor of five.
questions.trap: 5WL³/384EI is the simply supported case and WL³/192EI the fixed beam with a *point* load — all three live in the same family.
questions.trick: Fixed ends always stiffen: the deflection must be the smallest of the set.

questions.q: In plastic analysis, the segment between two successive plastic hinges is assumed to behave as:
questions.s: All the deformation is concentrated at the hinges, so the lengths between them rotate as rigid links and the collapse mechanism is a chain of them.
questions.trap: "Plastic" is the word in the question, which makes it the tempting answer; the plasticity is at the hinges, not between them.
questions.trick: A mechanism needs rigid links and frictionless hinges — same as any linkage.

questions.q: The rational method for peak runoff is applicable when:
o: The rainfall duration is at least the time of concentration
The rainfall duration is less than the time of concentration
The rainfall duration is half the time of concentration
Rainfall duration and time of concentration are unrelated
questions.s: Q = CIA assumes the whole catchment is contributing at once, which only happens once rain has lasted as long as the time of concentration.
questions.trap: A shorter, more intense storm feels like the worst case — but then only part of the catchment drains to the outlet together.
questions.trick: The peak needs every part of the catchment contributing simultaneously.
questions.mn: Duration ≥ tc, or the formula does not apply.

questions.q: Which pipe is normally located underneath the flooring of a building?
questions.s: Drainage runs by gravity, so it must be laid at the lowest level and falls continuously to the outside drain.
questions.trap: Water supply pipes are also concealed, but they are pressurised and are run in walls where they can be reached.
questions.trick: Gravity flow has to go underneath; pressure flow can go anywhere.
questions.mn: No pressure, no choice — put it low.

questions.q: For a given discharge, the two depths having the same specific energy are called:
questions.s: Alternate depths are the subcritical and supercritical pair on the same specific-energy curve. Conjugate (sequent) depths are the pair across a hydraulic jump, where energy is lost.
questions.trap: Conjugate depths are the near neighbour: same *momentum*, not same energy.
questions.trick: Energy curve ⇒ alternate. Momentum ⇒ conjugate.
questions.mn: Alternate = same E; sequent = same M.

questions.q: Euler's crippling load for a column with one end fixed and the other hinged is:
questions.s: The effective length is L/√2, so the load is twice that of a both-ends-hinged column.
questions.trap: 4π²EI/L² is the both-ends-fixed case and π²EI/4L² the cantilever — the whole family is offered together.
questions.trick: Multipliers run ¼, 1, 2, 4 as the restraint increases.
questions.mn: Quarter, one, two, four — free to fixed.

questions.q: The discharge passing over an ogee weir is proportional to:
questions.s: Q = (2/3)Cd√(2g)·L·H^(3/2) — the same three-halves power as any rectangular weir.
questions.trap: H^(2/3) is the same two digits the other way up, and is the exponent in Manning's equation.
questions.trick: Rectangular weir 3/2, triangular weir 5/2, orifice 1/2.

questions.q: Head loss is a minimum in a:
questions.s: Flow over a broad crest stays attached and runs nearly parallel to the surface, so very little energy is dissipated compared with a sharp crest where the nappe springs clear.
questions.trap: An ogee is shaped to the nappe profile and is also efficient, which makes it a reasonable but not the intended answer.
questions.trick: The more the jet separates, the more energy is lost.

questions.q: When three pipes are connected in series, the:
o: Discharge is the same through each pipe
Head loss is the same in each pipe
Velocity is the same in each pipe
Diameter is the same in each pipe
questions.s: Continuity requires the same discharge through every pipe, and the total head loss is the sum of the individual losses.
questions.trap: Equal head loss in each branch is the rule for pipes in *parallel* — the two arrangements are routinely swapped.
questions.trick: Series: Q common, h adds. Parallel: h common, Q adds.
questions.mn: Series shares flow, parallel shares head.

questions.q: In a roof truss, the ratio of the cost of purlins to the cost of trusses for an economical spacing is:
questions.s: The spacing is economical when the purlin cost is about twice the truss cost, which is where the total cost is a minimum.
questions.trap: Equal cost (ratio 1) is the intuitive optimum for two competing quantities, and is wrong here.
questions.trick: Purlins are the larger of the two costs at the optimum.

questions.q: The degree of static indeterminacy of a propped cantilever beam is:
questions.s: A fixed end gives three reactions and the prop one more; with three equations of equilibrium, 4 − 3 = 1.
questions.trap: A fully fixed beam is indeterminate to degree 3, and that figure is easily carried across.
questions.trick: Count the reactions, subtract three.

questions.q: A rectangular surface 2.5 m wide and 3 m deep has its upper edge in the free surface. The centre of pressure lies below the surface at:
questions.s: For a vertical rectangle with its top edge at the surface the centre of pressure is at 2h/3 = 2 × 3/3 = 2 m. The width does not enter.
questions.trap: 1.5 m is the centroid depth h/2 — the point the *force* acts about in a uniform field, not the centre of pressure.
questions.trick: Centroid at h/2, centre of pressure deeper at 2h/3.

questions.q: The design discharge of the under-sluices should be:
o: About double the canal discharge, and able to pass the winter flow
questions.s: Under-sluices are sized at roughly twice the canal discharge so they can scour the pocket, and they must carry the whole dry-weather flow.
questions.trap: "Equal to the canal discharge" is the tidy answer, but it leaves nothing spare for flushing sediment.
questions.trick: They must do two jobs — supply and scour — so they are oversized.
questions.mn: Twice the canal, plus the winter flow.

questions.q: The rate of filtration in a rapid sand filter is about:
questions.s: Rapid sand filters run at roughly 3000-6000 litres per hour per square metre — about 30 to 50 times the rate of a slow sand filter.
questions.trap: 100-200 L/hr/m² is the slow sand filter rate, and the two are the classic pair to confuse.
questions.trick: Rapid is some 30-50 times faster than slow.

questions.q: An inverted siphon sewer is also known as a:
questions.s: It dips below an obstruction and runs full under pressure, so it is properly called a depressed sewer — it is not a siphon at all.
questions.trap: "Pressure sewer" describes how it behaves and sounds like the technical name; the accepted term is depressed sewer.
questions.trick: The name "inverted siphon" is a misnomer, which is exactly why the question is asked.

questions.q: A disease that is widespread and can reach across the world is termed:
questions.s: Endemic is constantly present in an area, epidemic is a sudden local outbreak, and pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across countries or continents.
questions.trap: Epidemic also means "widespread"; the deciding word in the stem is the global reach.
questions.trick: Pan- means all, as in all the world.
questions.mn: Pan means all: a pandemic covers the planet.

questions.q: In a run-of-river diversion weir, the crest of the intake is provided:
questions.s: Setting the intake crest a few metres below pond level keeps the opening drowned so it draws clear water from below the floating debris and above the bed load.
questions.trap: Setting it at pond level looks economical but the intake would draw air and float rubbish straight in.
questions.trick: The intake wants water from the middle of the depth — below the scum and above the sediment.

questions.q: In the Unified Soil Classification System, the symbol SC represents:
questions.s: The first letter is the principal fraction (S = sand) and the second the modifier (C = clay). Silty sand is SM, well-graded SW and poorly graded SP.
questions.trap: SM (silty sand) differs by one letter and is the usual confusion.
questions.trick: Read the two letters in order: what it is, then what is in it.
questions.mn: S then C: sand with clay.

questions.q: The relationship e = wG holds when the soil is:
questions.s: The general relation is eS = wG; putting S = 1 for full saturation leaves e = wG.
questions.trap: Partial saturation is the general case and seems the safer answer, but it leaves S in the equation.
questions.trick: Substitute S = 1 into eS = wG and the stated form appears.
questions.mn: eS = wG — saturate and S vanishes.

questions.q: The seepage discharge through a flow net is given by:
questions.s: Nf is the number of flow channels and Nd the number of equipotential drops; the head h and permeability k complete it.
questions.trap: Inverting Nf and Nd gives a formula that is dimensionally identical and completely wrong.
questions.trick: More flow channels must mean more flow, so Nf belongs on top.

questions.q: The ratio of the settlement at time t to the final settlement is called the:
questions.s: The degree of consolidation U is a ratio and therefore dimensionless, running from 0 to 1 as consolidation proceeds.
questions.trap: The coefficient of consolidation cv sounds like the same thing but has units of area per time and governs the rate.
questions.trick: A ratio of two settlements must be dimensionless, which rules out every coefficient.
questions.mn: Degree = how far along; coefficient = how fast.

questions.q: A soil has a void ratio of 0.65 and a specific gravity of 2.65. The critical hydraulic gradient for a quick sand condition is:
questions.trap: Both 0.65 and 1.65 appear as intermediate values in that fraction, so a half-finished calculation lands on one of them.
questions.trick: The critical gradient of most soils is close to unity — a useful sanity check.
questions.mn: (G − 1)/(1 + e), and it usually comes to about 1.

questions.q: Coulomb's equation for the shear strength of a soil is:
questions.s: Shear strength is cohesion plus a frictional part proportional to the normal stress on the plane.
questions.trap: The minus sign is offered because effective stress analysis subtracts pore pressure — but that happens inside σ, not in front of the friction term.
questions.trick: More normal stress must give more strength, so the term is added.

questions.q: Terzaghi's bearing capacity of a square footing is:
questions.s: The shape factors for a square footing are 1.3 on the cohesion term and 0.4 on the width term.
questions.trap: 0.3 on the width term belongs to the *circular* footing, which shares the same 1.3 cohesion factor.
questions.trick: Square 1.3/0.4, circular 1.3/0.3, strip 1.0/0.5.

questions.q: Whistle-blowing by an engineer is justified primarily to:
o: Protect public safety and the public interest
Settle a dispute with the employer
questions.s: A professional's first duty is to the safety of the public; disclosure is justified when serious harm cannot be prevented through internal channels.
questions.trap: Personal grievance is the commonest motive in practice and the commonest wrong answer here.
questions.trick: Every code of ethics ranks public safety above the employer and above the engineer.
questions.mn: Blow the whistle for the public, not for yourself.
